questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=(x-4)^{2}(x+1)$ behave at the point $(4,0)$?

options.text: It touches the $x$-axis and turns back without crossing.
It cuts straight through the $x$-axis at an angle.
options.why: This is the behaviour at a zero of multiplicity $1$; here the multiplicity is $2$.

options.text: It flattens along the $x$-axis and crosses it.
options.why: Flattening while crossing needs an odd multiplicity of at least $3$.

questions.question_text: For $P(x)=(x+3)(x-2)^{3}$, what are the multiplicities of its two zeroes?

options.why: This reads the exponent $3$ on $(x-2)^{3}$ as $2$.

This swaps the exponents of the factors $(x+3)$ and $(x-2)^{3}$.

questions.solution_text:
The factor $(x+3)$ gives $x=-3$ with multiplicity $1$.
The factor $(x-2)^{3}$ gives $x=2$ with multiplicity $3$.

questions.solution_text:
The double zero at $x=2$ gives the factor $(x-2)^{2}$, and the simple zero at $x=-1$ gives the factor $(x+1)$.
$y=k(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$
$-8=k(0-2)^{2}(0+1)$
$-8=4k$
$k=-2$
$y=-2(x-2)^{2}(x+1)$

questions.question_text: How does the graph of $y=(x+2)^{2}(x-3)^{2}$ behave at its two $x$-intercepts?

options.text: It touches the $x$-axis and turns back at both intercepts.
It cuts straight through the $x$-axis at both intercepts.
options.why: This treats both zeroes as simple, ignoring the exponent $2$ on each factor.

options.text: It touches at $x=-2$ and cuts straight through at $x=3$.
options.why: This ignores the exponent $2$ on $(x-3)^{2}$, so it treats the zero at $x=3$ as simple.

options.text: It flattens along the $x$-axis and crosses at both intercepts.
options.why: This applies the behaviour of odd multiplicity at least $3$ to two zeroes of even multiplicity $2$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-2$ and $x=3$ each have multiplicity $2$.
Both multiplicities are even, so the curve touches the $x$-axis and turns back at both intercepts.
